articles.summary: Germany target of 'intensive' espionage, Merz says after suspected Russian spy arrest  BBCGermany’s Friedrich Merz warns of ‘intense’ Russian espionage after arrest  Financial TimesUkrainian man arrested in northeastern Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia  DW.comA suspected spy has been arrested in Brandenburg, Germany. He is alleged to have passed on military information to Russia. Several people have already been arrested in Germany this year on charges of s...
articles.full_text:
Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said after a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia.
Officials said the suspect, named as Vadym Y., had allegedly collected military-related intelligence from Germany.
Merz called the uncovering of the case a "success", but warned "let us not delude ourselves - the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level".
Several people alleged to be acting on behalf of Russia and other foreign powers have been arrested in Germany this year. Germany has been one of the leading European suppliers of weapons to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
The German Federal Prosecutor General's Office said on Thursday that Vadym Y., as he was identified under German privacy law, had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025.
It also said the Ukrainian man had collected information including "on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives".
He is due to appear before an investigating judge on Friday.
In January, a woman was arrested in Berlin suspected of gathering information for an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy.
Other arrests this year included a Romanian woman and a Ukrainian man accused of spying on an individual supplying drones from Germany to Ukraine, according to the prosecutor's office.
And, the former German spy chief August Hanning was arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power earlier this month. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.
Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D and accused him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents in exchange for money.
Speaking at the sidelines of a conference in Montenegro on Thursday, Merz said: "We will likely see more such cases in the coming months and years."
Merz reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier this month, including tackling hybrid attacks and hostile activity.
Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Russia.

articles.full_text:
The European Union (EU) has awarded its top human rights prize to the International Criminal Court (ICC), recognising its work to uphold international law and justice following growing pressure from the United States.
The European Parliament announced on Thursday that the ICC and its officials had won the 2026 Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. The award comes days after the administration of US President Donald Trump imposed new sanctions on the court.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said the decision recognised the court’s role in defending international law and justice.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” Metsola said.
Established under the Rome Statute, the ICC investigates and tries individuals accused of serious international crimes. These include genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
However, the court has faced increasing pressure from the Trump administration. Washington has accused it of seeking to prosecute Americans and US allies without their consent.
Although the United States is not a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC can investigate alleged crimes committed in countries that have joined the treaty. In 2020, the court opened an investigation into alleged crimes involving US personnel in Afghanistan.
In 2024, the ICC also issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza. Israel has rejected the allegations. Since then, the Trump administration has imposed several rounds of sanctions on the court and some of its judges.
The latest measures, announced on October 9, targeted the ICC’s ability to operate. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the sanctions were intended to restrict the court’s activities.
“Our message is clear: The United States and its people are not subject to the jurisdiction of the ICC,” Rubio said.
“Either the ICC will end its threats or we will end the ICC,” he added.
The ICC has rejected the sanctions, describing them as “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice” and “an assault on the rule of law.”
Thursday’s award marks another international recognition of the court and its officials this month. On October 9, former ICC judge and human rights expert Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
The ICC welcomed the European Parliament’s decision, saying the recognition came at a time of “unprecedented challenges.”
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” the court said.
The award, named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, is awarded annually to individuals and organisations that defend human rights and fundamental freedoms. The award ceremony is scheduled to take place in Strasbourg, France, in December.

As Washington leans on Ukraine to make a deal with Russia amid its diesel agreement ahead of the US elections, its European partners are meeting to keep it armed against deadly weapons.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he met Kongsberg CEO Eirik Lie and Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik in Oslo on 21 October to discuss more NASAMS air defenses, a day after meeting US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in the same city.
Washington has spent the past two weeks easing pressure on Russia and leaning on Kyiv, with a diesel deal, throttled Starlink, and talk of cutting intelligence, while Ukraine’s European partners move in the other direction. Russia pounds Ukrainian cities almost nightly, and the Norwegian-made NASAMS is one of the systems holding that barrage off critical infrastructure.
Kongsberg opened an office in Ukraine in 2025. Its NASAMS uses the AIM-120 AMRAAM missile built by the US defense giant RTX, the same firm behind the Patriot launchers that are Ukraine’s only means of downing Russian ballistic and hypersonic missiles. The same missile is also used in F-16s.
“They effectively protect our people and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks virtually every day,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that Ukraine is counting on additional defense support packages next month.
A European shield Ukraine wants tested this year
The visit also advanced a joint missile-defense project. Norway is actively involved in FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile program that Ukraine is helping to build.
“There are already first results in creating individual elements of the system. Today we determined where we can and must speed up to reach testing by the end of this year,” Zelenskyy said.
FREYJA now draws in 10 countries and is built around an interceptor missile designed to stop ballistic threats, a capability Europe largely lacks against Russia’s fastest weapons.
A push for satellites as Starlink falters
Zelenskyy also raised satellite communications amid the scandal over speed limitations on Elon Musk’s military Starlink service that disrupted a series of front-line missions.
“We discussed in detail the start of work on new satellite-communication capabilities for our soldiers,” the president said, adding that Kyiv would bring in partners able to support them.
The push comes after SpaceX throttled the StarShield military package Ukrainian drones use. Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps said the connection began dropping as drones moved at speed, negatively affecting their missions.

articles.title: Evidence of a Russian 'hybrid war' in Europe is vanishingly thin - Responsible Statecraft
articles.summary: Evidence of a Russian 'hybrid war' in Europe is vanishingly thin  Responsible StatecraftHow Russia Sees the World Now  Foreign AffairsWarsaw Security Forum Reflections  Progressive Policy InstituteThe Future of Russian-European Relations Is Bleak  Carnegie Endowment for International PeaceEurope Is Asking the Wrong Question About Russia’s Hybrid War  Foreign Policy
articles.full_text:
These days, barely a week goes by in Europe without a drone sighting, a fire or a power outage being blamed on Russia. We’re told that these incidents are all part of a relentless, and escalating, “hybrid war” that Moscow is waging against the continent.
Tensions escalated dramatically last month after Germany formally attributed to Moscow a “failed” drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport. But does the evidence support Western claims that Russia is engaged in a systematic hybrid war against Europe?
Various datasets and reports are regularly cited as evidence, including from Leiden University, the Soufan Center, the Associated Press and defense-related think tanks like the IISS, CSIS and GLOBSEC. Taken individually, each paints a bleak picture. Read side by side, however, they tell a very different story. For starters, the numbers don’t add up: depending on the report, Russia has launched between 52 and 255 hybrid attacks in Europe since February 2022, a fivefold discrepancy for what is supposed to be the same campaign.
The reason is that there is no agreed-upon definition of what a hybrid attack even is. The IISS itself admits that the term is “amorphous.” Some reports only count acts of physical sabotage; others include pro-Kremlin stickers, graffiti, peace demonstrations and even the Russian Navy passing through the English Channel. In other words, it is a concept that can be used to include almost anything. Moreover, in most cases, the evidence linking Russia is very weak or, in fact, non-existent. Evidence of Russian responsibility usually consists of news articles reporting that Western officials suspect so. If a government claims “Russia did it,” the case ends up on the list.
Yet many of the most widely publicized cases of alleged Russian sabotage — the “jamming” of the GPS signal of von der Leyen’s plane, the Baltic cable incidents in late 2024, a crashed DHL cargo plane, a fire at Heathrow Airport in 2025 — ended up collapsing upon basic scrutiny. In each case, Russian involvement was ultimately ruled out. The signal of von der Leyen’s plane, it turned out, was never lost. The Baltic cables were damaged by anchors dragged by Chinese- and Hong Kong-flagged ships, with investigators finding no evidence of intent. The DHL crash in Vilnius was caused by pilot error, and the Heathrow fire by a fault in a substation that had been identified years earlier but never fixed.But how many people actually know this, considering that such retractions generally receive a fraction of the coverage of the original allegations?
The same goes for the drone panic that swept Europe in the fall of 2025, when near-daily sightings caused the closure of several airports across the continent. Leaders openly blamed Moscow, yet virtually all the “Russian drone” sightings turned out to be unfounded: a Dutch investigation of some 60 incidents found “much panic and hardly any evidence of Russian involvement,” with many sightings turning out to be hobby drones, planes, helicopters, satellites or even stars.
Where Russian drones have indeed entered NATO airspace — in Poland, Romania, Moldova and Lithuania — this has almost always occurred near the Ukrainian border, during attacks on Ukrainian targets. Even the Lithuanian president has stated that the latest such incident was likely caused by a drone that veered off course because of Ukrainian jamming. This appears much more like fallout from the war next door than a deliberate campaign of incursions. There was one incident where a Russian drone was shot down deep in Polish territory, but even in this case Western intelligence officials “privately” admitted that the Russian incursion was probably not intentional.
And then there’s the Leipzig/Halle case. Following Germany’s official accusation of Russian involvement, NATO’s Secretary General Mark Rutte was quick to declare that “the evidence is clear.” This may very well be true, but since no evidence has actually been made public, we simply have to take the German authorities’ word for it. As a German professor told EUobserver, the attribution “may be plausible, but there is evidently no proof.”
Ultimately, once all the speculative and unproven “incidents” are set aside, what remains are a handful of demonstrable sabotage cases that have led to convictions, from a warehouse arson in London to torched buses in Prague,an IKEA fire in Vilnius and some GPS-tracker parcels sent toward Ukraine, allegedly to scout targets and transport routes for sabotage. Even in these cases, however, the courts have convicted low-level recruits, often contacted by anonymous handles on Telegram, and a connection to the Russian state or its proxies was established at a contested trial in only a handful of cases — notably the London warehouse fire and the GPS-tracker parcels in Germany — while elsewhere it rested on guilty pleas or closed hearings. But even assuming that Russia is indeed behind all these cases, the picture that emerges is one of few sporadic incidents with limited damage — hardly the “war” that European leaders routinely invoke.
Subscribe now to our weekly round-up and don't miss a beat with your favorite RS contributors and reporters, as well as staff analysis, opinion, and news promoting a positive, non-partisan vision of U.S. foreign policy.
So is this just a case of collective panic fuelled by click-addicted media? Or, given that the claims of a Russian “hybrid war” against Europe appear to rest on little more than propaganda, is there a concerted effort by the European Union-NATO establishment to condition citizens to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia?
The narrative clearly serves a variety of interests. For starters, it helps governments maintain support for an increasingly unpopular war in Ukraine and for a continental rearmament campaign that will require painful cuts to spending on other sectors. As a report by the Latvian Institute of International Affairs put it, the “nebulous tagline” of hybrid warfare would appear to be driven “by the need to goose flagging defense budgets and waning NATO cohesion.” It has worked: the drone panic has led to increased counter-drone spending at both the EU and NATO levels. Meanwhile, intelligence services have invoked the threat of sabotage to gain broader powers.
The specter of “Russian interference” also offers a broader authoritarian dividend, justifying everything from online censorship to the repression of dissent to election management — most egregiously in Romania, where an entire election was annulled because of an alleged Russian disinformation campaign for which no evidence of Russian involvement was ever provided. More recently, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, amid a push for greater EU ties, said it was “clear” that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, without providing any evidence, even though several investigations have found little or no evidence to support this claim.
One may conclude that, to the extent that a “hybrid war” is being waged against Europe, it is being waged by the EU-NATO establishment itself against its own population, in the form of a prolonged campaign of psychological warfare aimed at inflating the Russian threat.
What is most concerning is the risk that this becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. NATO countries continue to enable — through intelligence, satellite and targeting support — Ukrainian deep strikes on Russia, including on civilian infrastructure, and each attack makes Russian retaliation against NATO territory more likely. If and when such an attack comes, it would be framed as an unprovoked escalation of Russia’s ongoing “hybrid war,” leaving little room for European restraint.
This is a classic security dilemma. In such a climate, it would take very little for a “hybrid war” that so far largely exists only on paper to rapidly evolve into a hot war between nuclear-armed powers.
In Italy, the expression “strategy of tension” evokes a dark period, from the late 60s to the early 80s, in which intelligence services and secret paramilitary networks operating under NATO auspices inflated the terrorist threat to frighten the electorate, including by engaging in terrorist acts that in some cases were then blamed on the left. European leaders should be wary of reviving such a strategy.
This article draws on an in-depth investigation published on the author’s Substack.

articles.title: Technology, War, and the Limits of Innovation Power in the Middle East - The Washington Institute
articles.summary: Technology, War, and the Limits of Innovation Power in the Middle East  The Washington Institute
articles.full_text:
David Goodstone is the director of foreign policy at the Special Competitive Studies Project. Previously, he served in the Israeli Foreign Ministry, including as director of public affairs.
Eitan Danon is an Adjunct Senior Fellow at The Washington Institute.
Articles & Testimony
Both Israel and Iran have developed, adopted, and adapted drones and other technologies in innovative ways to yield success on the battlefield, but the broader strategic utility of these efforts remains uncertain.
Early on June 13, 2025, as Israeli F-35 jets entered Iranian airspace, a different kind of strike was underway—not from the sky, but from the ground inside Iran. For months, operatives had been smuggling drone components and missiles into the country through shipping containers, trucks, and suitcases, using commercial channels and largely unwitting business partners. Iranian state television later broadcast footage of a building near Tehran where components had been assembled into explosive-laden quadcopter drones. At zero hour, according to both Israeli and Iranian sources, the drones launched from concealed positions, destroying Iranian air defenses before a single Israeli aircraft was detected on radar.
Nine months later in Lebanon, a very different drone achieved its own record of success. Hezbollah operatives began flying first-person-view drones assembled from Chinese parts (bought on AliExpress) for a few hundred dollars each, steered via a fiber-optic cable that does not emit radio signals, making them immune to Israeli electronic jamming. The first drone’s impact was the result of years of intelligence work and can be used only once. The second drone could be built in a workshop by the thousands, without the same painstaking preparation.
The Twelve-Day War, Operation Rising Lion, was the Middle East’s most consequential military confrontation in decades. It was also only the opening round: On Feb. 28, 2026, the United States and Israel went to war with Iran again, in a wider campaign that remains unresolved. Both wars demonstrated what former Google CEO Eric Schmidt called “innovation power”: the capacity to not merely possess advanced technology but also to invent, adopt, and adapt it faster than an adversary. As Schmidt wrote in 2023, “If necessity is the mother of invention, war is the midwife of innovation.” Both Israel and Iran have applied innovation power in these wars, but in very different ways.
Israel’s innovation model is to execute bespoke military operations built on years of intelligence penetration. Historically, its technological edge has been most effective when deployed in short, sharp campaigns. For example, in June 1967, Israel’s air force destroyed most of Egypt’s air power on the ground in the opening hours of the war, relying on years of intelligence about airfields, radar gaps, and pilot routines. More recently, in 2007, Israel destroyed Syria’s undeclared nuclear reactor (confirmed by the International Atomic Energy Agency in 2026) in a single airstrike, having monitored the site without Syrian awareness, leaving no claim of responsibility and no escalation.
Iran’s model favors much longer, attritional conflicts, and gives primacy to cheap, expendable and scalable systems that any part of its proxy network can build. The goal is to impose heavy economic costs on its adversaries and outlast them. For instance, Iran’s support for Iraqi Shiite militias from 2003 onward through cheap weapons and financial support imposed asymmetric costs on U.S. forces and exemplifies Tehran’s use of attrition without need for decisive military victory.
In the ongoing conflict, each model has achieved a high degree of success on its own terms, which partly explains why the war has not concluded. Israel’s technology has achieved clearly defined tactical military goals (such as degrading Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile arsenal, leadership decapitation, and weakening the “Axis of Resistance”), but its durable security requires diplomatic agreements and painful political compromise. Iran’s model, which is cheaper to sustain, has secured the regime’s survival to date, but little beyond it: neither sanctions relief, nor restored deterrence, nor the proxy network it spent decades building.
The Israeli Model: Sophisticated Yet Unscalable
Since Oct. 7, 2023, in its war against Iran and its proxies, Israel has demonstrated both the reach and the ceiling of intricate operations underpinned by superior technology. Its successes have required near-perfect intelligence and significant resources, but this painstaking work makes them inherently unscalable.
In September 2024, in an audacious supply chain operation, Israeli intelligence remotely detonated thousands of handheld pagers and walkie-talkies used by Hezbollah, devices the group had procured specifically to avoid electronic monitoring. Former Mossad officers detailed how the agency created shell companies disguised as legitimate foreign manufacturers and placed untraceable explosives into batteries. This operation paralyzed Hezbollah command and control, but it also precipitated a shift in adversaries’ communications security practices from cell phones and pagers to couriers and handwritten notes.
Operation Rising Lion (Israel’s June 2025 campaign against Iran) and the 2026 campaign, Operation Roaring Lion, were the product of years of preparation. Over several years, Israel collected footage from hacked Tehran traffic cameras, analyzed it with artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted pattern-of-life tools, and used the results to direct the strike that killed Ayatollah Khamenei in February 2026. In its multifront war against Iran, Israel designed its long-term innovation to accelerate the kinetic phase of conflict. AI-assisted targeting systems, such as Gospel and Lavender, have enabled the Israel Defense Forces to compress intelligence cycles.
Cyber operations similarly achieved specific and immediate results. In June 2025, Israel-aligned hacking group Predatory Sparrow carried out cyberattacks on Iran’s largest crypto exchange, Nobitex, destroying $90 million in cryptocurrency, and on Bank Sepah, one of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC’s) principal banks. Yet, as the war renewed in February has shown, these disruptions did not fundamentally change Iran’s ability to project power, inflict global economic pain, or continue its nuclear program. Israel’s military innovation power is unmatched in a short campaign, but each operation is unique and hard to repeat once the adversary adapts, as Hezbollah did after the pager attacks.
The Iranian Model: Expendable by Design
Rather than matching Israel’s technical sophistication, Iran has deliberately exploited cost asymmetry, using technological adaptation to impose costs instead of achieving dominance. Its continued ability to close the Strait of Hormuz by leveraging geography, mines, and asymmetric maritime forces even without a conventional navy and air force exemplifies this strategy.
Most notably, Iran’s Shahed drone costs on average between $20,000 and $50,000 per unit, compared with the $3 million to $4 million for a Patriot missile interceptor. While not a precision munition, the Shahed has still wrought extensive damage on key U.S. bases in the region, including Naval Support Activity Bahrain.
Iran’s low-cost drones are as economic an innovation as they are technological; they forced rationing of one of its adversaries’ most expensive defense systems, and have driven some Arab Gulf states to replicate the Shahed’s cheap design as a model for drone warfare.
Iran’s proxies have also made effective, low-cost adaptations. Since March 2026, Hezbollah has deployed fiber-optic-guided first-person view drones that account for one-third of Israeli fatalities in southern Lebanon. Adapted from the Russia-Ukraine battlefield and assembled for as little as $300 to $500 per unit, they are immune to Israel’s electronic jamming, emit almost no radar or thermal signature, and have struck Merkava IV and V tanks despite their Trophy active protection systems, which were designed to stop missiles, not improvised drones. Israel’s Alma Research Center warned that “hundreds of dollars are defeating millions of dollars.” The drones’ supply chain requires no state-level capability to sustain: Components are purchasable on the China-based e-commerce platform AliExpress, assembled in workshops across southern Lebanon, and according to Lebanese customs data, fiber-optic cable imports through Lebanese ports nearly doubled between 2023 and 2024.
Iran’s playbook has long been one of strategic extortion to generate leverage disproportionate to its conventional capabilities, and its technological approach is no exception. From the hostage crisis in 1979 to the kidnapping for ransom of dual nationals to the mining of the Strait, coercive leverage, not decisive battlefield victory, has been Iran’s consistent operating model. In carrying out its internet blackout in January 2026, the regime denied adversaries visibility into the country as it killed an estimated 30,000 or more people, according to senior officials, in a matter of days while simultaneously suppressing protesters’ ability to mobilize.
Inverted Information Warfare Costs
Iran has applied the same logic to the domain of information warfare, where the cost asymmetry is even starker. According to the Canadian government, this content reached 83 million views in its first month and spread across TikTok, Instagram, and Telegram. articles.title: Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz - The Guardian
articles.summary: Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz  The GuardianSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.
In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.
Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.
Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.
Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.
Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.
According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.
Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel.
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.
Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.
Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.
“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.
Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.
Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.
Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.
The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.
“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.
From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.
Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.
Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.
“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

articles.summary: ‘Freeze and Stop!’ Zelensky Tells Fox News’ Brian Kilmeade He Would ‘Accept’ End of War Along Current Frontlines  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday he would accept freezing the war along its current frontlines, publicly embracing a ceasefire framework that would leave Russia in control of territory it presently occupies while negotiations continue.
Appearing on Fox & Friends, Zelensky was pressed by co-host Brian Kilmeade on whether he would accept an agreement that effectively stopped the fighting where the battlefield stands today.
"Would you accept a peace deal that freezes everything the way it is right now, where you still keep 75% or more of your country?" Kilmeade asked.
"Yes," Zelensky replied. "Right now, we have to freeze and I think this is [the] real way to end this war."
He added: "We call it ceasefire or 'stop killing' as President Trump called it. Freeze and stop."
Zelensky stressed that such a halt would be only the first step, arguing that any deal would need firm guarantees to prevent Russia from restarting the war: "And, of course, this is [the] minimum [of] what we need from Russia today. Then we will go to the president and Europeans and ask [for] security guarantees."
"The most important is peace and also security [of] peace," Zelensky continued. "Not to be afraid that occupation will come back, aggression will come back, killings will come back. We have to stop this and that's why [we need] freeze and talks. And security guarantees from the United States and prosperity from our partners for innovation of our lives."
His remarks come as President Donald Trump intensifies pressure on Kyiv to reach a settlement with Moscow. Trump has repeatedly promoted the idea of stopping the fighting along the existing front, while Russia has continued to demand control over additional Ukrainian territory, including areas of Donetsk that its forces do not currently occupy.
The two sides remain far apart on the final status of occupied territory and the shape of any postwar security arrangement. Moscow has also continued to oppose Ukrainian NATO membership, while Kyiv has pressed Washington and European governments for binding guarantees against renewed Russian aggression.
Zelensky framed a frontline "freeze" as a way to move from combat into negotiations rather than a final territorial settlement, and help rebuilding Ukraine.
"We need 9.5 million people which are broad everywhere," Zelensky said. "We need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country."
Watch above via Fox & Friends.

Zelensky stated that he is open to accepting freezing the current frontline in Ukraine, which he also referred to as a ceasefire, and noted that Ukraine will ask for security guarantees from the US President Donald Trump and Europe after the ceasefire.[1] Some sources inaccurately presented Zelensky’s October 21 Fox News statement as a new Ukrainian concession despite Zelensky long offering this concession since 2024. Zelensky first publicly spoke about a ceasefire deal that would include de facto Russian control of Ukrainian territories without de jure recognition on November 29, 2024, and has since reiterated his openness to an immediate ceasefire.[2] Zelensky has repeatedly presented various ceasefires and peace proposals, which the Russian officials have continuously rejected and have not yet offered any meaningful concessions toward peace negotiations.[3]
Senior Kremlin officials reiterated Russia’s long-standing unwillingness to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations while attempting to present Ukraine and Europe as the main obstacles to peace in Ukraine.
Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov provided his commentary following the October 21 meeting between US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St.
Petersburg.
[4] Ushakov stated that Witkoff briefed Putin on the Ukrainian and European peace proposals from Witkoff’s meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo, Norway, on October 20, and Putin noted that those proposals have “little that was useful” in resolving the war in Ukraine.
Ushakov separately told Kremlin journalist Pavel Zarubin on October 21 that Russia “is not completely satisfied” with the “nuances” in European behavior.
[5] Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov claimed on October 21 that Russia’s position on an energy ceasefire with Ukraine has not changed and added that Russia “needs peace, not a ceasefire.
”[6] Russian State Duma International Affairs Committee member Denis Kravchenko claimed on October 21 that progress on resolving the war in Ukraine is possible but only if Russia’s “fundamental demands are met.
”[7] The Kremlin officials’ October 21 statements effectively rejected Ukraine’s and Europe’s peace proposals by labeling them as insufficient, indicating Russia’s intransigence in its war objectives and continued unwillingness to accept Zelensky‘s concessions.
The Kremlin officials continue reiterating the Kremlin’s long-standing narrative that Ukrainian and European leaders are the main obstacles to peace, despite Russia’s continuous rejections of Ukrainian and European ceasefire and peace proposals on any terms that fall short of fulfilling Russia’s goals of Ukraine’s complete capitulation despite the fact that the Russian military is unable to achieve those goals on the battlefield.
[8]
The Kremlin is attempting to negotiate under the false assumption that Russia holds the strategic initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite ample evidence to the contrary. Ushakov claimed that Putin presented Witkoff with an “objective picture” of the frontline situation, where Russian forces have “complete strategic initiative.”[9] Ushakov further claimed that Russian forces are conducting a “relentless offensive” in all key areas of the frontline. Official Russian claims of Russian successes do not reflect the current battlefield realities, however, and are reflective of the pervasive culture of lying within the Russian military. Russian high-ranking military commanders also routinely present exaggerated Russian advances as part of Russia’s systematic cognitive warfare effort to portray Russian forces as making sweeping advances and Ukrainian defenses as collapsing.[10]
Russia is failing to achieve its battlefield objectives in reality, however, and Ukrainian counteroffensive operations have operationally defeated the planned Russian offensive to complete the seizure of Donetsk Oblast – Putin’s self-defined objective since 2022.
[11] ISW has observed evidence to assess that Ukrainian forces have liberated about 1,080 square kilometers of territory since January 1, 2026.
ISW has observed evidence to assess that Russian forces have net gained about 73 square kilometers since January 1, 2026, and suffered a net loss of about 73 square kilometers since September 1, 2026.
Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman direction defeated the northern pincer of Russia’s planned encirclement of Donetsk Oblast and liberated at least 277 square kilometers, continuing to generate cascading effects for Russian offensive operations in neighboring sectors.
[12] Ukraine has proven its ability to contest the operational initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans on numerous occasions throughout 2026 and will likely be able to continue to do so in the coming months, assuming continued Western military support, intelligence sharing, and unimpeded access to Starlink and Starshield communications technologies.
Putin has set no fewer than 16 deadlines for the seizure of Donetsk Oblast since 2022 and Russian forces have failed to meet every single one.
[13] Putin’s battlefield perceptions remain divorced from the reality of Ukraine’s defensive abilities, Russia’s own degraded offensive capabilities, and the difficult and expansive terrain that Russian forces must still fight through to achieve Putin’s strategic goal in Donetsk Oblast.
Pro-war Russian sources continue to complain about how official Russian reports are deeply exaggerated and are not representative of battlefield reality.
[14]

Russia released US citizen Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg on October 21.[18] Russian authorities imprisoned Hubbard on October 7, 2024, for allegedly serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces (which Russian authorities criminally charged Hubbard for) and sentenced him in 2024 to seven years in prison during closed court proceedings.
The United States, Ukraine, and Russia will likely hold trilateral peace negotiations around November 10. Ushakov claimed on October 21 that Putin told Witkoff that Russia is “in principle” ready to resume trilateral negotiations between Russia, Ukraine, and the United States around November 10 and suggested that such negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.[19] The United States, Ukraine, and Russia last held trilateral negotiations in February 2026.[20]

articles.title: Surveillance and ‘constant paranoia’: Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow - BBC
articles.summary: Surveillance and ‘constant paranoia’: Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow  BBC
articles.full_text:
- Published
"Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.
US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.
But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.
They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.
Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.
Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.
"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."
The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.
Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.
"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.
Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.
The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".
Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.
One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.
Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police.
One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear.
Not everyone can deal with the pressure.
One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months.
'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats'
In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre Lévy.
He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be.
The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible.
And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies.
Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country.
But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning.
After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Еven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers.
One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'."
Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses.
A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase.
"It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour."
Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".
Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.
This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."
Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."
But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.
"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."
Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.
But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.
"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

articles.title: Christa Pike’s IV team warned vein might be ‘blowing’ before failed execution - The Guardian
articles.summary: Christa Pike’s IV team warned vein might be ‘blowing’ before failed execution  The GuardianExecution staff worried IV site might have ‘blown’ during Christa Pike’s execution attempt  CNNOne in three Americans back second execution attempt after failed one, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds  ReutersChrista Pike Speaking in Full Sentences After Botched Execution  TMZChrista Pike’s surprising recovery after failed execution sparks legal debate as poll shows low suppor...
articles.full_text:
The Tennessee execution team tasked with setting an intravenous line in the arms of the death row prisoner Christa Pike through which she could be injected with a lethal dose of pentobarbital repeatedly warned that her vein might be “blowing”, before they went ahead with the procedure, her lawyer has revealed.
Members of the intravenous (IV) team used up to 10 needles as they sought to establish a line through which Pike could be killed with a massive dose of the sedative. About 20 minutes into the attempt, they began discussing among themselves whether the prisoner’s vein “might be blowing”.
Two unidentified members of the team began poking the site through which they were trying to set up the line, and both agreed that they couldn’t tell whether they had succeeded in finding the vein. “One of them said something like: ‘It’s either blood or blown, I need to know,’” the lawyer’s new account says.
The potentially critical new details of how Tennessee’s execution team failed to kill Pike, 50, on 30 September are contained in the most detailed account yet given by Pike’s lawyer Randy Spivey.
In a declaration that was released as part of separate legal proceedings, Spivey gave a minute-by-minute chronology of Pike’s ordeal, which he personally witnessed in the death chamber.
The account suggests that the IV team was racked by doubts even before the pentobarbital began to flow, as they struggled to find a vein for almost an hour. The search began at 6.35pm that evening, and was completed at 7.24pm, at which point the team left the chamber assuming everything was going according to plan.
But Pike remained alive, making snoring and choking sounds.
The execution was eventually called off, and after 10 days in hospital Pike was returned to prison in Nashville. She is the only prisoner in modern times to survive a full dose of a lethal injection drug.
Though she can now talk and walk, her long-term prognosis is still unknown. The gruesome events of her failed execution have prompted nationwide soul-searching about the death penalty in the US, and forced the Republican governor of Tennessee, Bill Lee, to call off all executions in the state pending a review.
Spivey’s blow-by-blow chronology gives agonizing new details about the lengths to which the IV team went to find a vein, as well as their profound anxieties about whether they were doing the right thing. A person on the IV team named by Spivey as “member two” first expressed the fear that Pike’s vein might be blown at 6.53pm.
The team then discarded the 20-gauge needle that they had been using, saying: ‘“It’s not long enough. What is the longest you’ve got?”
Three minutes later, at 6.57pm, member two repeated it “might be blowing”. Spivey reported: “Member two and IV team member 3 inspected the insertion site and poked it. Both said that they ‘can’t tell’.”
Despite the uncertainty, the IV team agreed among themselves that they had established a line just two minutes later, only to discover that it was not, in fact, properly working. “I need to work again,” member two said, pulling the needle out of Pike’s left arm. “It appeared to be severely bent,” Spivey records.
At 7.08pm member two called on the team to think again. “Let’s regroup,” he said. They began checking Pike’s right arm again, and poking around the insertion site. At 7.13pm, member two told Pike directly that they “have it”, and the injection of pentobarbital that they thought would kill her was set to begin.
The revelations of so many doubts and foiled efforts to find a line, including the critical fears that her vein might have blown, lend added weight to one of the most prominent theories that have emerged for how the execution failed and Pike survived. Had the drug entered her bloodstream at such a extreme dose she would almost certainly have died, but if her vein burst, the pentobarbital would have been diverted into her arm tissue, causing her severe injuries but falling short of killing her.
As Spivey noted in his chronology, at 7.34pm Pike cried out: “I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns.”
Spivey’s detailed minute-by-minute account is attached as an exhibit in a new legal motion filed on behalf of Tony Carruthers and other death row prisoners. Tennessee attempted to execute Carruthers on 21 May, but he too survived after the execution team failed to find a vein in more than 30 minutes.
Carruthers’s lawyers have asked permission from the Davidson county chancery court to file a supplemental complaint challenging Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol. They made an initial complaint in March 2025 in which they warned that the prisoner could face a torturous death by pentobarbital poisoning because the team administering the lethal drug were “incompetent, insufficiently trained, insufficiently dedicated to doing their jobs, and/or insufficiently attentive”.
As such, they warned, the execution ran an unacceptable risk of violating constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The failed executions in May, and Pike’s subsequent failed execution in September, bear out the lawyer’s advance warnings, the new motion asserts. “The specific failures that Mr Carruthers and Ms Pike endured were predicted, in detail and at length,” the new motion states.
Kit Thomas, an attorney for the death row plaintiffs, said: “Instead of addressing the problems in the 2025 Protocol when we identified them last year, the Tennessee Department of Correction and the Attorney General’s Office doubled down on secrecy and refused to make changes. The result was just as we predicted: extreme pain and suffering for our clients, in botched execution attempts that also inflicted lasting harm on victims’ families, corrections staff, and media witnesses, among others.”
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of her friend Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 at the time of the murder, and spent the next almost three decades in solitary confinement.

articles.title: Iran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Iran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response  Al JazeeraIran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war  YahooIran's IRGC Navy says seven vessels hit, warns US of wider response  ReutersOctober Marks Highest Number of Strait of Hormuz Attacks  USNI NewsSea mine crisis re-emerges in Strait of Hormuz as Tehran urges Washington to accept deal  Fox News
articles.full_text:
Iran says that seven oil tankers have been struck and sustained damage in the Strait of Hormuz, the largest single-day toll for the waterway since the United States and Israel started their war against Iran on February 28.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight. The other three were disabled after striking mines.
The claims could not be independently verified, and the report did not provide details about possible casualties or the tankers’ flags.
The IRGC also warned that it could strike US bases across the Middle East if Washington moves to help tankers transit other parts of the strait.
“The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region,” the IRGC said in a statement on its Sepah News website. “This is a serious warning.”
Iran claims control over Hormuz, a strategic shipping route through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before war broke out. It regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the strait without its authorisation.
But the US military has been escorting vessels through the waterway in increasing numbers, with Iran responding by stepping up attacks.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of oil prior to the US Midterm Election”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, he added: “They are making up fake hits, mines, and everything else because more oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict.”
A US Central Command spokesperson, speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera, also called Iran’s mine claims incorrect.
The spokesperson said US forces have cleared the international shipping lanes of mines and that Iran is using missiles and drones.
The strait remains open, the spokesperson said, with 95 percent of vessels getting through.
The attacks, the spokesperson added, show Tehran’s “desperation” under the US blockade, which cuts Iran off from the resources it needs to rebuild the military capabilities the US has said it destroyed.
Americans want ‘relief’ from war costs
“The number of ships and tankers attacked every single day is increasing, and Iran is saying it is continuing to do this because they are not going to allow any change in that situation,” said Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran.
“They have full control over the Strait of Hormuz right now, they say.”
Vall said there is also talk in Tehran about an imminent escalation in the war, with the Iranians expecting the US to attack even before US midterm elections in early November.
“The IRGC army chief has boasted that Iran is more ready than anytime before, and has produced enough weapons and equipment to wage a symmetrical war against the United States,” he said.
Reporting from the US White House, Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett said: “Striking Iran does not appear to serve any Republican interests”, adding that pre-election polls tell the same story for Trump’s political party.
“What we’ve seen in surveys in recent months, and as of today, is that most Americans want relief from their tax money going to pay for any potential war with Iran that is ramped up,” Halkett said.
“There is real frustration over the rising cost for everyday Americans, given the rising fuel prices that have occurred as a result of this conflict … As a result, the US president is having to make the case.
“The pressure is on the president, and it’s not just from the opposition party,” she said. “It is also from within the Republican Party as well.”

articles.summary: Tension along Korean border fuels concern as Kim Jong Un's sister issues "not a threat, but a clear warning"  CBS NewsNorth Korea's Kim Yo Jong warns South Korea, says border loudspeakers to be ready within days  ReutersNorth Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea  NBC NewsAcross The Border: An Area Awaiting Rural Development  38 NorthNorth Korea threatens to "mercilessly eliminate" US-backed South Korean forces as i...

Tension on the Korean Peninsula is once again ratcheting up, with calls for immediate talks between to avert an accidental military confrontation.
It follows hostile back-to-back statements from – the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un – who said loudspeakers broadcasting anti-South Korea propaganda would be activated within days along the .
She also warned Seoul of "the most horrible and distressing situation" if South Korea continues what Pyongyang called interference in North Korean internal affairs.
"This is not a threat," she said, "but a clear warning."
On Wednesday, Kim Yo Jung joined senior military officials to visit fortification sites along the border, where she said North Korean tactical units had taken up positions. She accused South Korean forces of broadcasting warning messages and firing warning shots at multiple locations near the border.
South Korea acknowledged that its forces had fired warning shots, calling them "legitimate and defensive measures."
North Korea expert Bob Carlin, a former U.S. State Department analyst who took part in negotiations with Pyongyang and has followed the country closely for four decades, told CBS News that Kim's statements about "tactical units" are a cause for concern.
"Whether these have heavy weaponry or not, this represents a change in the situation along the front," said Carlin. "Kim Yo Jung also spoke of the possibility of 'deploying more tactical strike means.' This sounds more like artillery and battlefield missile units, and if the decision has been made to move these up, it will be an even more serious change along the front lines."
Swirling in the background of the rising tension this week were online rumors that North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, had died after suffering a brain hemorrhage. The regime discredited the uncorroborated claims by having state media release photos of the 42-year-old dictator touring a clothing and footwear exhibition in Pyongyang with his wife and teenage .
Kim's father, Kim Jong Il, died in 2011 at the age of 69 from a heart attack. His death was only announced to the public two days later. There has been much speculation over who would succeed Kim Jong Un if he were to die suddenly.
Within the South Korean intelligence community, Kim Ju Ae, who in public in recent years, has been labeled the likely heir apparent. She would be the fourth generation for the Kim dynasty.
But experts believe Kim's sister has been asserting her authority recently, too, and appearances like this week's are part of that effort.
Yang Moo-jin, chair professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said Kim Yo Jong's frequent public appearances "serve two purposes: demonstrating to Kim Jong Un that she is working diligently, while also asserting her own profile and influence toward both South Korea and the United States."
Yang said the focus for both governments now should be on resolving the current tension along the demilitarized zone that separates North and South Korea — where some 28,500 U.S. forces are still based more than 70 years after the .
"The issue of North Korean troops moving southward takes precedence," he told CBS News. "The realistic and rational way to resolve the problem is not through further border fortification, but by sitting down together and finding a mutually acceptable solution through dialogue."
The demilitarized border zone, or DMZ, was established as part of the 1953 armistice agreement between the U.S.-backed South and the China- and Soviet-backed North that ended hostilities in the Korean War.
Since 2024, North Korea has reinforced its side of the DMZ with mines, barriers and more fencing to establish what it calls a permanent border with South Korea.
Last month, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded by what Seoul says were North Korean mines planted as part of those fortifications.
South Korea announced Thursday that it would inform the United Nations Security Council that the mine blasts, in its view, represent a violation of the armistice. Seoul has demanded an apology and the initiation of dialogue with Pyongyang to prevent further escalation.

articles.title: The European Parliament honored the court that issued an arrest warrant for Putin: who was awarded the 2026 Sakharov Prize - Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.summary: The European Parliament honored the court that issued an arrest warrant for Putin: who was awarded the 2026 Sakharov Prize  Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.full_text:
Kyiv • UNN
The European Parliament honored the ICC for defending international law and justice. For Ukraine, the decision strengthens support for the investigation of war crimes.
On October 22, the European Parliament announced the laureate of the 2026 Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. The award was presented to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and its officials for defending international law and justice.
UNN explains the history of the prestigious award, its laureates, and why this year's Sakharov Prize is important for Ukraine.
Sakharov Prize 2026: who became the laureate and what they received the award for
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola announced the decision to award the prize to the ICC during a session in Strasbourg. The deputies greeted the decision with a standing ovation.
The European Union is founded on respect for multilateral cooperation and international institutions, and the prize recognizes the court's important work in protecting international law and justice. The European Parliament supports the principle of independent investigations into the most serious crimes
ICC President Tomoko Akane, for her part, expressed gratitude for the honor, emphasizing that it had taken on special significance at a time when the institution and its staff were facing unprecedented challenges. She called for support for the court's independent and impartial work.
It should be noted that the decision to present the award to the ICC coincided with the imposition of U.S. sanctions on the court. Washington introduced the restrictions several hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize.
What is the Sakharov Prize, and why is it considered one of Europe's most prestigious awards
The European Parliament has presented the Prize for Freedom of Thought since 1988. It is named after physicist and Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, who advocated for human rights. It is the European Union's highest distinction for work in the fields of human rights, democracy, and freedom of expression. It may be awarded to both individuals and organizations. Candidates are nominated by political groups or at least 40 Members of the European Parliament. After three finalists are selected, the final decision is made by the Conference of Presidents, which includes the president of the European Parliament and the leaders of the political groups. Laureates may receive financial support of 50,000 euros.
International Criminal Court: what the organization does and why it was honored in 2026
The ICC began operating in 2002 under the Rome Statute. It is a permanent international court that considers individual responsibility for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and, under special conditions, the crime of aggression. It intervenes when national courts are unwilling or unable to properly investigate such crimes.
Unlike the International Court of Justice, which resolves disputes between states, the ICC brings cases against specific individuals, including military and political leaders. At the same time, it has no police force of its own: the arrest of suspects depends on the cooperation of states.
Who else was nominated for the Sakharov Prize in 2026
The finalists were selected on October 19 by the European Parliament's Foreign Affairs and Development committees. In addition to the ICC, Tanzanian opposition politician, lawyer, and human rights defender Tundu Lissu was included on the shortlist. He is being held in custody on charges of treason, for which the death penalty is possible.
The third nomination went to Iranian sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi as symbols of those persecuted by the Iranian authorities. Taraneh was sentenced to death in connection with the protests, while Romina was given a lengthy prison sentence. Members of the European Parliament condemned the politically motivated sentences and demanded that they be overturned.
Of the six nominees, physician Hussam Abu Safiya, El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, and the Israeli organization Standing Together did not make it to the final.
The Sakharov Prize and Ukraine: why the European Parliament's decision is particularly significant
For Ukraine, everything related to the ICC's activities is important primarily because it was this international institution that issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, the Commissioner for Children's Rights. They are suspected of war crimes related to the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.
In 2024, the ICC also issued arrest warrants for Russian commanders Sergei Kobyلاش and Viktor Sokolov, and later for Sergei Shoigu and Valery Gerasimov. The cases concern, among other things, alleged crimes committed during strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
In addition, as of January 1, 2025, Ukraine became a full-fledged party to the Rome Statute. Therefore, the ICC's work is important for investigating crimes committed on the territory of Ukraine.
It is important to understand that the Sakharov Prize does not change the court's jurisdiction or ensure the immediate detention of suspects. However, this international award undoubtedly strengthens political support for the institution from which Ukraine expects justice.
The political context of the award: U.S. sanctions against the ICC and the position of the European Union
On October 9, 2026, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump extended sanctions to the ICC as an institution, following earlier restrictions against individual judges and prosecutors. Washington explained its position by citing its rejection of the court's jurisdiction over Americans and the ICC's actions concerning U.S. allies. One of the causes of the conflict was the arrest warrants issued in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.
The sanctions regime provides for restrictions on financial transactions and cooperation with U.S. companies. At the same time, some transactions were authorized for a 180-day transitional period. The ICC called the sanctions an attempt to obstruct independent justice.
The European Union criticized Washington's decision and said it was ready to support the court. The European Commission is discussing, among other things, the use of a so-called blocking statute, which could protect European companies from requirements to comply with certain foreign sanctions. As of October 22, no decision had been made to activate this mechanism. The award does not replace practical protection for the court.
Who received the Sakharov Prize previously, and which of the laureates were Ukrainian
Ukraine's history with the prize is embodied in two European Parliament decisions. In 2018, it was awarded to Ukrainian director Oleh Sentsov, who was then imprisoned in Russia. In 2022, the award was given to the "brave people of Ukraine" for resisting Russia's full-scale aggression and defending freedom and democracy.
Among the laureates of the prestigious international award were also Nelson Mandela, Malala Yousafzai, the Iranian movement "Woman, Life, Freedom," and Jina Mahsa Amini (2023). In 2024, the prize went to Venezuelan opposition figures María Corina Machado and Edmundo González Urrutia. The 2025 laureates were journalists Andrzej Poczobut from Belarus and Mzia Amaghlobeli from Georgia.
When will the 2026 Sakharov Prize be presented, and what does the award mean for the future of international justice?
The 2026 Sakharov Prize award ceremony is scheduled for December 16. It will take place in Strasbourg during a plenary session of the European Parliament.
For Ukraine, the significance of this event lies primarily in confirming European support for the principle of individual accountability for the gravest international crimes. Whether solidarity will become practical assistance will be shown by the subsequent decisions of the EU and the parties to the Rome Statute.
A reminder
Two journalists, Andrzej Poczobut and Mzia Amaghlobeli, imprisoned in Belarus and Georgia, received the 2025 Sakharov Prize. They were recognized for freedom of thought and speaking out against injustice while being imprisoned on fabricated charges.

Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel said he's skeptical of the US war with Iran and does not believe the United States should have launched it, putting the major Republican donor at odds with President Donald Trump over one of the administration's defining foreign policy decisions, POLITICO reported.
Thiel's remarks, delivered on October 12 at a private event, are his most explicit statements to be revealed publicly about the war with Iran and come less than two weeks before the midterm elections in which Trump's party is grasping to maintain power in Congress. The audio of Thiel's comments was obtained by Decoded by POLITICO from a lecture earlier this month.
"I'm skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it," Thiel said. "There were a lot of mistakes that were made."
Thiel added, "Maybe we don't have the hard power. Maybe we're going to lose the soft power war."
In the full lecture, Thiel made clear his strong opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars. Despite his criticism of the Iran war, Thiel highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president.
Still, Thiel's break over the war represents one of the most important examples to date of a fierce Trump ally sharing deep concerns about the conflict.
The comments were part of Thiel's lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has documented since their start this fall. In the latest lecture, Thiel issued extensive warnings about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on comments from Bush-era figures Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney.
"I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late," Thiel said. "And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran."
Thiel also discusses meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after the October 7 attack, where he said he asked the president about his plans in Gaza. Thiel said Netanyahu told him, "I can't just Dresdenize it," referring to the Allied bombing of the German city of Dresden during World War II that killed roughly 25,000 people.
The first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016, and then have a high-profile speaking role at the Republican National Convention that year, Thiel was also the biggest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance's Senate campaign in 2022. POLITICO reported in March that Vance was "skeptical" of the U.S. striking Iran in the lead-up to the beginning of the war.
Representatives for Thiel and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
